body:
What is malnutrition?

Malnutrition occurs when nutrient or energy intake is insufficient, excessive or imbalanced in relation to the body's needs. It includes undernutrition, deficiencies of vitamins or minerals, and problems associated with excess energy intake.

Malnutrition is not the same as simply feeling hungry. A person may eat enough food to satisfy hunger but still lack iron, iodine, vitamin A or another essential nutrient. Similarly, someone may consume excessive calories while receiving too little dietary fibre or too few micronutrients.

How deficiency diseases develop

A deficiency disease develops when the body receives or can use too little of an essential nutrient for long enough to impair normal function. The problem can arise from an inadequate diet, difficulty absorbing the nutrient, illness or increased nutritional needs.

For example, a diet lacking vitamin C over time can lead to scurvy. A diet lacking sufficient iodine can contribute to thyroid-related problems. Iron deficiency can reduce haemoglobin production and cause anaemia.

The appearance of symptoms varies. Some deficiencies develop gradually and may initially cause general symptoms such as tiredness or poor growth. Others are associated with distinctive signs, such as difficulty seeing in dim light or bleeding gums.

Protein-energy malnutrition

When the body receives inadequate energy and protein, especially during childhood, normal growth and tissue maintenance can be seriously affected. Severe forms have traditionally been described using the terms marasmus and kwashiorkor.

Marasmus

Marasmus is characterised by severe wasting, with marked loss of body fat and muscle. The person becomes extremely thin because available energy and tissue reserves are insufficient.

Kwashiorkor

Kwashiorkor is characterised by nutritional oedema, particularly swelling affecting both feet. Oedema means abnormal accumulation of fluid in body tissues. A child with nutritional oedema may not appear extremely thin, even when seriously malnourished, because retained fluid can conceal weight and tissue loss.

Important qualification: Both marasmus and kwashiorkor are forms of severe malnutrition. The traditional statement that kwashiorkor results only from protein deficiency while marasmus results only from calorie deficiency is an oversimplification. Multiple nutritional and health factors may contribute.

Wasting, stunting and micronutrient deficiency

  • Wasting: low weight in relation to height or length, reflecting acute undernutrition in the usual child-nutrition classification.
  • Stunting: low height or length in relation to age, generally reflecting long-term restrictions on normal growth.
  • Micronutrient deficiency: inadequate availability of a vitamin or mineral, which may occur even when calorie intake appears sufficient.

These are different ways in which poor nutrition can affect health. They should not be treated as identical terms.

Nutrition and illness can affect each other

Undernutrition may reduce the body's ability to respond to infection. Repeated illness, particularly diarrhoea, can then reduce food intake or interfere with nutrient use and absorption. This creates a cycle in which illness worsens nutritional status and poor nutritional status increases vulnerability to further illness.

Prevention

Preventing nutritional deficiencies requires an adequate and varied diet, safe drinking water, hygienic food preparation and appropriate healthcare. Some people need additional nutritional support because of pregnancy, rapid childhood growth, illness or difficulty absorbing nutrients.

Severe wasting, swelling of both feet, pronounced weakness or suspected significant deficiency requires medical assessment. A single food item or home remedy cannot be assumed to correct every cause of malnutrition.

Prelims focus

  • Malnutrition includes insufficient, excessive and imbalanced nutrition.
  • Micronutrient deficiency can occur despite adequate calorie intake.
  • Marasmus is characterised by severe wasting.
  • Kwashiorkor is characterised by nutritional oedema, commonly involving both feet.
  • Wasting and stunting describe different patterns of poor growth.
  • Trap: Nutritional oedema can conceal serious tissue loss.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Ch. 2, Components of Food, printed pp. 15–16; World Health Organization, Guideline on the Prevention and Management of Wasting and Nutritional Oedema in Infants and Children under 5 Years, 29 December 2023, overview; WHO, Management of Severe Acute Malnutrition in Children 6–59 Months of Age with Oedema, updated 9 August 2023; WHO, Implementation Guidance on the Management of Wasting and Nutritional Oedema, 17 September 2026, overview; WHO, Diarrhoeal Disease, 7 March 2024, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Malnutrition and the Development of Deficiency Diseases

body:
What is a balanced diet?

A balanced diet provides the body with all essential nutrients in appropriate quantities, together with adequate dietary fibre and water, to support health, growth and normal functioning.

Balance does not mean eating exactly the same quantity of every nutrient or food group. Requirements differ according to age, sex, physical activity, body condition, health status and life stage. A growing child, a pregnant woman and a physically active adult may require different amounts and combinations of foods.

The principles of a healthy diet

Adequacy

Food should supply sufficient energy, protein, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water for the body's needs. A diet that supplies sufficient calories but insufficient iron or vitamin A is not nutritionally adequate.

Diversity

Eating a variety of foods helps provide nutrients that are absent or present in small quantities in individual foods. Cereals and millets, pulses and beans, vegetables, fruits, milk or suitable alternatives, and nuts and seeds contribute different nutrients.

Balance and moderation

Energy intake should be appropriate for the person's needs. Foods containing excessive added sugar, salt or unhealthy fats should not routinely replace nutrient-rich foods. Regular physical activity also supports health.

A practical meal using foods familiar in Gujarat

A nutritious Gujarati meal can be prepared using affordable, locally available ingredients. For example, a meal may include bajra rotla, moong or tuvar dal, a seasonal green vegetable, curd and water. Fruit such as guava, papaya or amla can be included during the day, while a modest portion of groundnuts or other nuts and seeds contributes additional nutrients.

The nutritional contributions of these foods overlap, but their main roles are easy to understand:

  • Bajra rotla: supplies carbohydrate for energy, along with fibre and some minerals.
  • Dal: contributes protein for growth and repair, together with carbohydrate, fibre and minerals.
  • Green leafy vegetables: contribute vitamins, minerals and fibre.
  • Curd: contributes protein and calcium.
  • Guava or amla: contributes vitamin C and other nutrients.
  • Water: supports hydration and normal body functions.

This is an illustration of food-group variety, not a fixed diet prescription or a claim that one meal fulfils every daily requirement. Adequacy depends on the amount eaten and the full day's diet.

Millets are nutritious, but variety still matters

Millets such as bajra, jowar and ragi are commonly described as nutri-cereals because they can contribute fibre and minerals in addition to energy. However, millets are not complete foods by themselves. A diet consisting only of millet preparations would still lack adequate amounts of several nutrients. Combining millets with pulses, vegetables and other food groups improves dietary variety.

Preserving nutrients during food preparation

Food preparation affects nutritional value. Some nutrients, particularly vitamin C, are sensitive to heat. Repeated washing of rice or pulses, or washing vegetables after cutting them, can remove some water-soluble nutrients.

Fruits and vegetables should be washed properly before consumption, preferably before cutting. Safe cooking remains important because it can improve digestibility and reduce the risk of foodborne illness. The aim is to retain useful nutrients without compromising hygiene.

Food quality is not determined by price

Expensive foods and supplements are not automatically necessary for a balanced diet. Pulses, roasted chana, groundnuts, seasonal vegetables, whole grains, millets and locally available fruits can make substantial nutritional contributions.

Frequent consumption of foods rich in added sugar, salt or fat but poor in protein, fibre and micronutrients can contribute to an imbalanced diet. Such foods may provide many calories without meeting the body's full nutritional requirements.

Prelims focus

  • A balanced diet contains essential nutrients in appropriate quantities, along with fibre and water.
  • Nutritional requirements vary with age, activity, health and life stage.
  • Cereals or millets combined with adequate pulses help improve overall protein quality.
  • Millets such as bajra, jowar and ragi are nutritious grains but are not complete diets by themselves.
  • Excessive washing after cutting vegetables and prolonged heating can reduce some nutrients.
  • Trap: A diet containing enough calories may still be deficient in vitamins or minerals.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Ch. 2, Components of Food, printed pp. 13–16; GCERT, Standard 6 Science (Curiosity), Ch. 3, Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body, printed pp. 46–54; ICMR–National Institute of Nutrition, Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, Guidelines 1, 6, 7 and 8, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Balanced Diet: Principles and Practical Indian Food Choices

body:
Why is digestion necessary?

Food contains complex substances such as starch, proteins and fats. Many of these cannot be absorbed and used by the body in their original form. Digestion breaks complex food components into simpler substances that can be absorbed through the digestive tract.

Digestion involves mechanical actions, such as chewing and mixing, and chemical actions carried out by digestive enzymes. An enzyme is a biological substance that speeds up a particular chemical reaction.

The 5 main stages of animal nutrition

  1. Ingestion: taking food into the body.
  2. Digestion: breaking complex food into simpler substances.
  3. Absorption: movement of digested nutrients through the intestinal wall into the body's transport systems.
  4. Assimilation: use of absorbed nutrients by cells for energy, growth and repair.
  5. Egestion: removal of undigested and unabsorbed material as faeces.

Digestion and assimilation are different. Digestion produces absorbable substances, whereas assimilation refers to their use after absorption.

Organs involved in human digestion

Mouth

Food enters through the mouth, where teeth break it into smaller pieces. Salivary glands produce saliva, which moistens food and contains salivary amylase. This enzyme begins the digestion of starch.

Oesophagus

The swallowed food passes through the oesophagus, or foodpipe. Rhythmic muscular movements called peristalsis move food towards the stomach.

Stomach

The stomach stores and churns food while mixing it with gastric juice. Gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid, mucus and digestive enzymes. Hydrochloric acid creates an acidic environment that supports the action of pepsin, an enzyme that begins protein digestion. Mucus helps protect the stomach lining.

Small intestine

The small intestine is the main site where digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats is completed. It receives secretions from the liver and pancreas, and its wall also produces digestive substances.

  • Liver: produces bile, which helps in fat digestion.
  • Gallbladder: stores and concentrates bile before its release into the intestine.
  • Pancreas: releases pancreatic juice containing enzymes that help digest carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
  • Intestinal glands: contribute enzymes that complete the digestion of food.

Bile helps break large fat droplets into smaller droplets through emulsification, increasing the surface area on which fat-digesting enzymes can act. Bile itself does not contain digestive enzymes.

The end products of digestion include simple sugars such as glucose from carbohydrates, amino acids from proteins, and fatty acids and glycerol from fats.

Absorption through intestinal villi

The inner lining of the small intestine contains numerous finger-like projections called villi. These increase the surface area available for absorption. Absorbed nutrients enter blood or lymphatic vessels and are transported to different parts of the body.

Large intestine, rectum and anus

Material that remains undigested or unabsorbed passes into the large intestine. The large intestine absorbs remaining water and some salts. Faeces are stored in the rectum and expelled through the anus.

Where digestion and absorption differ

ProcessMain locationKey fact
Starch digestion beginsMouthSalivary amylase acts on starch
Protein digestion beginsStomachPepsin acts in an acidic medium
Digestion of major food components is completedSmall intestinePancreatic and intestinal enzymes act
Most absorption of digested nutrientsSmall intestineVilli increase absorption area
Absorption of remaining water and saltsLarge intestineHelps form faeces

Key distinction: The liver produces bile, the gallbladder stores it, and pancreatic enzymes carry out important chemical digestion. The small intestine is the principal site for nutrient absorption; the large intestine is particularly associated with absorption of remaining water and salts.

Prelims focus

  • Salivary amylase begins starch digestion in the mouth.
  • Pepsin begins protein digestion in the acidic stomach.
  • The liver produces bile; the gallbladder stores it.
  • Bile emulsifies fats but does not contain digestive enzymes.
  • Villi of the small intestine increase the surface area for nutrient absorption.
  • Trap: Digestion and absorption are different processes, even though both occur extensively in the small intestine.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Ch. 2, Nutrition in Animals, printed pp. 11–20, copy marked 2018–19; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Ch. 5, Life Processes, section 5.2.4, printed pp. 84–86; NCERT, Biology, Class 11, Ch. Digestion and Absorption, sections on the digestive system and digestion of food.]
